title: Scoliosis in teenagers
intro: Scoliosis is a sideways curvature of the spine. The most common type, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, appears during the growth spurt of puberty without a known cause. Most curves are mild and only need monitoring, while larger curves may be treated with a brace or, rarely, surgery.

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: When viewed from behind, a healthy spine is straight. In scoliosis it curves to the side, often with a twist of the vertebrae so that one shoulder, shoulder blade or hip appears higher, or a rib hump appears when bending forward. It is more common in girls and tends to run in families. Poor posture or heavy backpacks do not cause it.

sections.heading: Symptoms and finding it
paragraphs: Scoliosis usually causes no pain. It is often noticed by a parent, at school screening or at a routine visit because of uneven shoulders or waist. Back pain in a teenager with scoliosis should be assessed, as other causes can be present. Doctors measure the curve from an X-ray with the Cobb angle.

sections.heading: Monitoring
paragraphs: Mild curves are monitored with check-ups every few months while the teenager is growing, and many do not progress. Doctors assess the risk of progression using age, sexual maturity, curve size and the years of growth remaining. Exercises designed for scoliosis, guided by a physiotherapist, may help some patients improve posture and trunk strength.

sections.heading: Brace treatment
paragraphs: For moderate curves in growing children, a brace can reduce the risk of progression and the need for surgery if worn for the prescribed number of hours daily. Braces are usually worn under clothing, and teenagers need support, understanding and encouragement. Regular check-ups ensure fit and effectiveness.

sections.heading: Surgery and everyday life
paragraphs: Surgery, in which vertebrae are fused with rods, is considered for large or fast-progressing curves. It is a major operation with risks, but results are good. Most teenagers with scoliosis can do sports and daily activities normally, and exercise is encouraged. Emotional support helps, because body image concerns are common.

examples.title: Spotting a curve
examples.text: Imagine you notice your daughter's shoulder blade sticks out when she bends forward. You could arrange an examination with her paediatrician or an orthopaedic doctor.

examples.title: Wearing a brace
examples.text: Suppose your teenager has to wear a brace for most of the day. You might talk about when it is worn, arrange comfortable clothing and involve school and sports teachers.
